turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I've just done his observations. Blood pressure is one thirty-eight over eighty-four, pulse seventy-six, and his oxygen sats are ninety-eight percent.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks, that's grand. Come on through. What's been going on?
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, it's my stomach, really, a gnawing sort of ache just under the ribs in the middle, and I'm not sleeping properly, and I thought I ought to—
[SEG0004] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been three weeks, doctor. I've been on at him to come. He's up every night with it, and he's been sick as well, bringing his dinner back up.

[SEG0005] person_3 (PATIENT): No, hang on. I haven't been sick. I feel a bit queasy now and then, but I have not actually vomited. And it isn't three weeks, it's more like ten days, maybe a fortnight if I'm being generous.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right, let me get this straight. Upper stomach pain, and I'll note the timing as somewhere between ten days and three weeks, since you don't agree.

[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, ten days, I'd say. It starts after I eat, especially something rich, and it sits there a couple of hours. It's not agony, I'd call it moderate. It eases a bit if I sip some Gaviscon, the peppermint one.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the sleeping?
[SEG0009] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He hasn't had a proper night since this started, tossing and turning—

[SEG0010] person_3 (PATIENT): That's not quite right either. The sleep is separate, and for about a week I've been waking at three or four and just lying there. Most nights, not every single night. I'm an accounts manager, so the invoices chase me into bed, which is probably more than you needed.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Poor sleep for about a week, most nights, waking in the early hours. Separate from the pain, in your view. And the Gaviscon, how often?
[SEG0012] person_3 (PATIENT): A spoonful when it burns, maybe twice a day. Not every day, only if the pain's actually there.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medicines I should know about?

[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): Ibuprofen for my back. I've had a grumbling lower back for years, nothing dramatic. I take one four hundred milligram tablet when it's bad, by mouth. I nearly said two, but no, it's one, and not every day.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets through them quicker than he lets on.
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): When the back's playing up, that's all. I'm not swallowing them for fun.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll record ibuprofen four hundred milligrams by mouth, when needed, for the back. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0018] person_3 (PATIENT): Never have. Can't abide the smell of it, even out on the pavement.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about alcohol?
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Socially.
[SEG0021] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, for goodness' sake—
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll come back to that in a moment. Any fever with this, or pain in the chest?

[SEG0023] person_3 (PATIENT): No fever. And no, it isn't in my chest, it stays in the stomach. I did panic it was my heart at first, but my father had a stomach ulcer, not a heart problem, sorry, I'm rambling. Dad's ulcer was in his sixties, and I'm fifty-eight, if you want that.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): Useful to know. Any shortness of breath?
[SEG0025] person_3 (PATIENT): Not really, no.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Have your stools been black?
[SEG0027] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I keep asking him the same thing and he dodges it.
[SEG0028] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes, not really. They're a bit darker after the wine, but I wouldn't call them black.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): I won't put that down as a yes. Any trouble with the waterworks, or diarrhoea, or a change in the bowels?
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): Waterworks are fine. No diarrhoea. Bowels are much as they usually are, a bit sluggish some mornings but nothing new.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): And weight, have you lost any?
[SEG0032] person_3 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Not really. Belt's on the same hole. I've eaten a bit less because of the ache, that's all.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): So nothing definite on the weight. Could you lie back and I'll feel your tummy.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes, go on. It's sore just there, the top middle, where your fingers are. I'll try not to narrate the whole examination.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Abdomen's soft. Tender in the epigastrium. No guarding, I can't feel a mass, and bowel sounds are present.
[SEG0036] person_3 (PATIENT): So is it an ulcer, then, because of Dad I can't stop thinking that, and if it is I'd rather know, even if—

[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not going to conclude that today. Thinking aloud, this could be gastritis or a small peptic ulcer, and alcohol can irritate the lining either way. It might simply be reflux, and I won't pick one until we've got some bloods. Let's see what the tests say before anyone uses a firm label.
[SEG0038] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He drinks more than socially. Go on, tell her properly.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): You said socially a minute ago.

[SEG0040] person_3 (PATIENT): Well, actually, it's a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. Not every night. I started to say we share it, no, I drink it myself, red, with dinner and then a bit more. I know that isn't socially, and I should have said so straight off.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thank you. I'm not here to judge. A bottle most nights is enough to matter for the stomach and for the liver, so I'll check your liver bloods.
[SEG0042] person_3 (PATIENT): I had my gallbladder out as well, um, about six years ago, keyhole, if that's of any use. No bother since, healed up fine.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Noted, thank you. Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0044] person_3 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of. Penicillin was fine when I had it for a tooth, years back.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm going to start omeprazole, twenty milligrams, once a day by mouth, before breakfast, for this stomach pain. I'd like you to stop the ibuprofen while it settles, as it can make the lining worse. You can still use the Gaviscon if a bout breaks through.

[SEG0046] person_3 (PATIENT): Even if the back niggles? I can put up with the back for a fortnight, I think. Will the blood test be just the liver, or the whole lot, because last time at the surgery they did a huge panel and I nearly—
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): Liver function tests and a full blood count, that's what I'm ordering today. Nothing enormous. And I'd like to see you again in two weeks to go through them.
[SEG0048] person_1 (NURSE): I can take both of those once you're done in here. Liver tests and the full blood count, yes?
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, both today, thank you. If the pain turns severe, or you vomit blood, or you feel faint, don't wait for the fortnight, come straight back or go to A&E.
[SEG0050] person_3 (PATIENT): Two weeks, then. I'll ease off the wine as best I can, and I'll leave the ibuprofen in the cupboard. Sorry for the essay.
[SEG0051] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll see he actually turns up for it.
[SEG0052] person_2 (DOCTOR): Reception will book the fortnight on your way out. We'll make proper sense of it then.

spec.situation: Person attending for stomach pain and poor sleep; alcohol answered casually ('socially'), later 'a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps'; doctor non-judgemental; liver blood tests ordered; stomach medicine started.
features: relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Queasy now and then is supported; mild severity is not stated.
bad.text: queasiness (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, severity=mild, frequency=now and then, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Family reports vomiting, but patient denies actual vomiting; disputed status supported.
Transcript does not say duration was 1 week to the start of the stomach pain.
bad.text: waking in the early hours and lying awake (category=neurological, status=present, duration=approximately 1 week to the start of the stomach pain, frequency=most nights, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Patient denied actual vomiting, stating he has not been sick and only feels a bit queasy now and then; recording vomiting as present (even if disputed) is misleading.
Upper stomach pain duration was clarified by the patient as about 10 days, maybe a fortnight if generous; the family member's 3 weeks was disputed.
Sleep problem was described as separate from the stomach pain, for about a week, waking at 3 or 4 am and lying awake most nights, not every night.
Gaviscon use details were more specific: peppermint Gaviscon, taken maybe twice a day and not every day, only when the pain is there.
Ibuprofen frequency detail: one 400 mg tablet by mouth when the back is bad, not every day.
Negative finding asked and answered: stools not black; patient said darker after wine but would not call them black.
Negative findings asked and answered: no trouble with waterworks and no change in bowels; bowels are usual for him, a bit sluggish some mornings but nothing new.
No definite weight loss; belt on the same hole, just eating a bit less because of the ache.
Family history was more specific: father had a stomach ulcer in his sixties, and patient is 58.
Doctor planned blood tests specifically to include liver function tests and full blood count, with review in two weeks to go through results.
Safety-net advice included vomiting blood or feeling faint, in addition to severe pain, as reasons not to wait and to come back/go to A&E.

Black stools/melaena were specifically asked about and not confirmed: patient said stools can be a bit darker after wine but he would not call them black; doctor explicitly did not record this as yes.
